title: Irenaeus against contempt for matter
hook: against those who called the world evil, he defended bodies and creation

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeds of the Word: Justin finding truth sown in the philosophers. Your line was seeds everywhere. What seed did you find in someone unlike you? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

An aching back. Bad news on the phone. Someone you love, sick. For some teachers in the early church, there was a tidy explanation for all of it: the world itself was the mistake. Matter was a trap, built by a lesser power, and the body was a cage. Salvation meant secret knowledge, and the secret was how to get out. Later writers group these teachers under the name Gnostic, though they did not all agree. A bishop in Lyon, in Gaul, thought they had it exactly backward. His name was Irenaeus, and he wrote a long work called Against Heresies. Today, Irenaeus against contempt for matter.

Irenaeus starts where the Bible starts. Genesis closes the sixth day with a verdict: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Not a mistake. Very good. Rocks, rivers, animals, bodies. Then he points to the center of the faith: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." If flesh were a cage, why would God's own Word step into it? Then he points to the table. Bread comes from the earth and wine from the vine, and in the Eucharist, he argues, these ordinary things receive the word of God and become the gift of Christ's body and blood. If wheat and grapes can carry that, how can anyone say the flesh is worthless? And he points forward, to the resurrection. The Apostles' Creed confesses the resurrection of the body: not a soul set loose, but a body raised. For Irenaeus, the whole story is God making, and then God mending what was made, not God throwing it away. He sums it up in a line, here in paraphrase: the glory of God is a human being fully alive, and human life is seeing God. Paul says something close: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" A temple, not a cage. Some churches draw on this when they care for the sick, bless fields and gardens, and bury their dead with care. Bodies matter. Bread matters. The ground under your feet matters.

Here's the practice: care for your body. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and move slowly up. Your legs. Your back. Your hands. Your shoulders. Your face. Don't judge anything you find, just notice. Where is it tired? Where is it carrying something? Then pick one small act of care for today. A glass of water. A walk around the block. An early night. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body, the one Genesis would call very good. The bell holds the time.
Irenaeus against contempt for matter. A bishop defending creation and the body as God's good work, against teachers who called the world a trap.

notes: The index word is truncated ('Irenaeus against contempt for matter'); kept exactly as the validator requires. The word screen and voice use the full title. Suggest fixing the index word in a separate owner-approved edit.

Gnostic teachings summarized (matter made by a lesser power, the body as a cage, salvation by secret knowledge) and hedged with 'often grouped under the name Gnostic'; confirm fair to the range of groups Irenaeus opposed.
The Eucharist argument is paraphrased from Against Heresies 4.18.5 and 5.2.2–3; confirm wording 'receive the word of God and become the gift of Christ's body and blood' is acceptable across churches.
'Gloria Dei vivens homo' is paraphrased in the voice as 'a human being fully alive', a common modern rendering; the Latin is 'living'. Confirm.
'Best known in a Latin translation' (trapdoor): Against Heresies survives complete in Latin, with Greek fragments; confirm phrasing.
'It's one reason churches care for the sick, bless fields and gardens' links practice to the theology loosely; confirm.

Editor pass: claims-rule cuts: 'often grouped' and 'their ideas spread' (now 'later writers group these teachers under the name Gnostic, though they did not all agree'); 'a line people still quote'; 'Christians confess' (now 'the creeds confess the resurrection of the body'); 'one reason churches...' (now 'some churches draw on this'); the trapdoor's manuscript claim ('best known in a Latin translation') replaced with the text of 4.20.7 itself. 'Ends its first creation story' corrected to 'closes the sixth day', since Genesis 1:31 is not the end of that account (2:1–3).
Audit pass: "The creeds confess the resurrection of the body" made precise: the Apostles' Creed says "resurrection of the body"; the Nicene Creed says "resurrection of the dead".
